You can use your result from Homework 9 Problem 1. Problem 2. Let A ∈ Mn×n(R) be a matrix with distinct positive eigenvalues λ1, . . . , λn. (i) How many real matrices B satisfy A = B2? (ii) How many real matrices B satisfy A = B3? (iii) How many complex matrices B satisfy A = B3? (Include the real matrices B in your count) Hint: Find the eigenvalues of B. Is B diagonalizable? What are the eigenvectors of B? Hint: We have seen in Lecture 9 that x3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x − ω)(x − ω2) has 3 distinct roots in C where ω = −1+ √3i 2 . Problem 3. Suppose T ∈ L(V ) is invertible and v1, . . . , vn is a basis of V with respect to which the matrix of T is upper triangular, with diagonal entries λ1, . . . , λn. Show that the matrix of T −1 is also upper triangular with respect to the same basis v1, . . . , vn, and its diagonal entries are 1 λ1 , . . . , 1 λn . Problem 4. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). (i) Suppose A is nilpotent, i.e. there is an integer k > 0 such that Ak = 0, show that An = 0 and that A is diagonalizable if and only if A = 0. (Note that the integer k is arbitrary and need not satisfy k ≤ n.) (ii) Suppose A ∈ Mn×n(C) and A4 = A. Show that A is diagonalizable over C. What are the possible eigenvalues of A? (iii) Suppose mA(x) = xm + am−1xm−1 + · · · + a0. Show that A is invertible if and only if a0 ̸= 0. If A is invertible, show that A−1 = − 1 a0 (Am−1 + am−1A m−2 + · · · + a2A + a1I).
